I would be happy to implement the sections in the way that is implied by heading elements according to the spec. 

### Advantages
- I have been trying to parse the source file so that features in one of my own programs could rely directly on the spec itself, but the parsing is more difficult with a flat structure.
- The spec, by definition, describes a standard, but it does not follow this standard itself. It would be really nice if people could look at the code of the spec to see how they can write HTML themselves! (at least, the outputed HTML from the source)

My suggestion would be to do this in the source itself. If you give me the go ahead on this, this is what I will do. 

FYI: This would be my first issue on this standard.

@mithrayls sorry for the delay in responding! I'm excited that you're interested in tackling this. We'd love your help.

I'd be happy to have you do this in the source itself. However, I'd feel most comfortable if you did it in an automated fashion somehow. It would be much easier for any reviewer to audit a script, than it would be for them to audit the hundreds of lines of diffs (all of which are just adding `<section>` or `</section>`). Do you have any thoughts on that?

P.S.

> The spec, by definition, describes a standard, but it does not follow this standard itself. It would be really nice if people could look at the code of the spec to see how they can write HTML themselves! (at least, the outputed HTML from the source)

To be clear, not using `section` is totally valid HTML, and still follows the standard. A flat list of elements is fine. But, some more structure does help other programs, as you mention.

My natural starting point would be to use the [parse5](https://www.npmjs.com/package/parse5) library, iterate through the nodes and surround the h tags with section tags where I hit a boundary of equal or greater importance. Another approach, which I actually already successfully used to solve my own personal problem parsing the standard involved the use of a multiline regex but that might be considered unprofessional ;-)

No worries about the delay. I noticed you blogging about the spammy Pull Requests! This was an awkward moment for me as I knew I had this issue outstanding with you ! :-p

[EDIT] I realize the source meets the standard it describes, but I think it would not meet *best practices* of semantic HTML? At any rate, section tags would make it easier to parse and locate sections.

[EDIT] I've tried both parse5 and jsdom to parse and then serialize, as well as with and without passing it through a prettifier, but the diff is very large due to what seem to be very minor changes, such as whitespace between tags. For this reason, it might be better to go with the regex idea. Unless there is some kind of canonical prettification for the source code that will allow me to make changes to a parsed tree without creating a huge diff of irrelevant changes(the diff changes actually make the *source* harder to read by getting rid of helpful formatting)? I think that would be useful for making automated changes. I think a canonical prettifier would make more sense.

Is this still desired? I've been looking at it a bit.

Do you know whether Wattsi can handle source with `section` elements?

This would still be desired! Although I'm not sure if we want to go with the all-h1 route or just do a one-time update of the source. If we did the all-h1 route then I think these days I'd prefer doing that in the [Rust preprocessor code](https://github.com/whatwg/html-build/tree/main/src) instead of in Wattsi.

Wattsi should have no problem with section elements, as it has a full HTML parser.

> This would still be desired!

Okay, I'll look at it some more.

> Although I'm not sure if we want to go with the all-h1 route or just do a one-time update of the source. If we did the all-h1 route then I think these days I'd prefer doing that in the [Rust preprocessor code](https://github.com/whatwg/html-build/tree/main/src) instead of in Wattsi.

So in this scenario, the source would have h1-h6, the Rust preprocessor would change those to all h1 (in some internal data structure?), and then what? In your original post, you said "We can't keep them as all-`<h1>`s", which I thought meant that the 'rendered' spec couldn't be all-h1. If that's the case, what's the benefit of having all-h1 transiently in the build process?

(To be clear, I don't think I want to get into the build tools, so the only contribution I'm considering is changes to the source file, but I'd still like to understand what you meant.) 

> Wattsi should have no problem with section elements, as it has a full HTML parser.

Well, I wasn't worried that Wattsi could *parse* them, just wondering if they would confuse subsequent processing.

> So in this scenario, the source would have h1-h6, the Rust preprocessor would change those to all h1 (in some internal data structure?), and then what? In your original post, you said "We can't keep them as all-`<h1>`s", which I thought meant that the 'rendered' spec couldn't be all-h1. If that's the case, what's the benefit of having all-h1 transiently in the build process?

In that scenario, we would change all `hN`s in the source to `h1` and the preprocessor would convert them into the correct `hN` based on section nesting level. This would avoid the `N` getting out of sync with the section nesting level.

Okay, *that* makes sense to me. So when you said "If we did the all-h1 route then I think these days I'd prefer doing that in the Rust preprocessor code...", by "doing that", you meant converting *from* all-h1 rather than converting *to* all-h1, right?

But I'm still puzzled about "I'm not sure if we want to go with the all-h1 route or just do a one-time update of the source." Because the all-h1 route that you just described does involve a one-time update of the source.

----

It sounds like there are roughly 3 approaches that have been discussed in this issue:

1. Leave the source more-or-less as is, and modify the build process to inject `<section>` elements.

   - "However, that would probably be a pain to implement."
 
2. Edit the source to add `section` tags, and leave the build process as is.

   - Problem: Spec editors will have to manually match `<section>` and `</section>` tags. (There are a couple ways we could maybe make this easier.)

   - Problem: In time, it could happen that the `N` of an `hN` element disagrees with its nesting level within the `section` hierarchy. (Possible solution: modify the build process to complain about any disagreement.)

3. Edit the source to add `section` tags & convert `hN` tags to `h1`, and modify the build process to convert all the `h1` back to `hN`, based on the `section` hierarchy in the source.

   - This ensures that the `hN` headings are in sync with the section hierarchy.

   - This will probably improve the spec-authoring experience.

   - Do the `h1->hN` conversion in the Rust preprocessor so that Wattsi gets the input it expects, doesn't have to change.

(Note that we could do (2) in the short term and progress to (3) in the longer term.)

> Okay, _that_ makes sense to me. So when you said "If we did the all-h1 route then I think these days I'd prefer doing that in the Rust preprocessor code...", by "doing that", you meant converting _from_ all-h1 rather than converting _to_ all-h1, right?

Yes.

> But I'm still puzzled about "I'm not sure if we want to go with the all-h1 route or just do a one-time update of the source." Because the all-h1 route that you just described does involve a one-time update of the source.

I apologize, I agree I wasn't very clear.

I think you've summarized the options well. But for the record, in my most recent messages I was envisioning two paths: your 2 vs. your 3. I forgot that my OP suggested your 1.

I think 2 for now, and maybe 3 in the future if we find it painful to maintain, seems very reasonable.

Okay, sounds good. So I'll focus on inserting `section`s into the source. --- Re spec editors having to manually match `
` and `
` tags, I thought of a couple things: - The tags could be indented according to their depth in the section-hierarchy. E.g., a top-level `section` would have its start tag + end tag flush-left, a second-level `section` would have its tags indented 1 space, etc. So you can find a matching end-tag by searching for (e.g.) ```/^ <\/section>/``` - Each section tag could be accompanied by a comment that gives the section name. (Or maybe just the end-tags, since the start-tags will have a nearby heading with the section name.) The drawback with both is that they have to be maintained by spec authors, so are at risk of not being maintained. However, the build process could be modified to complain about discrepancies. Does either of these appeal, or do you have another idea? --- Also, the status quo spec has a `div`-hierarchy. How do you want it to 'interact' with the `section`-hierarchy? For example, say the current spec had this: ```

Stuff

before

within

One

blah

Two

blah

``` A simple approach would insert `section` tags like so: ```

Stuff

before

within

One

blah

Two

blah

``` (Changes in indentation are only to help understand the example structure.) As far as I can tell, it's valid to have a `section` containing a `div` containing a `section`. However, it doesn't seem to be what people expect: in examples I've found, a `section` directly contains its sub-`section`s (if any), without any intervening elements. Direct section-containment also seems like it would be easier on software processing the spec. So I suggest that, when a `div` would (in the simple approach) contain a `section`, what should instead happen is that the `div`'s attributes are transferred to the `section`, and the `section` is removed from the `div`. So, the example would be: ```

Stuff

before

within

One

blah

Two

blah

``` (In the common case where a `div` doesn't contain anything other than `section`s-to-be, it won't appear in the sectioned spec.)

> Does either of these appeal, or do you have another idea?

Personally, I think neither of these pulls their weight in terms of maintenance cost.

> Also, the status quo spec has a `div`-hierarchy. How do you want it to 'interact' with the `section`-hierarchy?

I think section containing div containing section would be fine. But your version also seems OK, and perhaps more intuitive.

Note that the `<div w-nodev>` and friends are stripped at build time, and don't appear in the ultimate output. So the output would have directly-nested sections.

> > Does either of these appeal, or do you have another idea?
> 
> Personally, I think neither of these pulls their weight in terms of maintenance cost.

Okay, so what indentation would you like for `section` tags? The `body` tags are indented 1, and most of the top-level content has tags indented 2.

> I think section containing div containing section would be fine. But your version also seems OK, and perhaps more intuitive.

I'll do the latter, and we'll see how it looks.

> Okay, so what indentation would you like for `section` tags? The `body` tags are indented 1, and most of the top-level content has tags indented 2.

I would use 2, similar to the `<div w-nodev>`s.

I've got a candidate spec-with-sections, but (as I feared) it confuses the build process. Even though the build says "Success!", it produces only single-page documents for the `dev` and `multipage` versions. I think what's happening is that the introduced `section`s are preventing Wattsi from 'seeing' any of the `split-filename` attributes, so it never knows to start a new file.

E.g., as an experiment, try putting `<section>...</section>` tags just around the `Acknowledgments` section, which has `split-filename="acknowledgements"`. The build will complete with success, but won't generate `dev/acknowledgements.html` or `multipage/acknowledgements.html`.

Oh dear, I'm so sorry I didn't realize that would happen. And yes, I can confirm that's what's happening. The Wattsi code which assumes `split-filename` attributes appear at top level is at https://github.com/whatwg/wattsi/blob/b9c28036a2a174f7f87315164f001120596a95f1/src/wattsi.pas#L2670-L2701 .

In some cases the fix is relatively easy: move the `split-filename` attributes from the `<h2>`s to the `<section>`s. However, this doesn't work when we're splitting at the `<h3>` level. (Which has always been a bit weird, but the alternative is very large documents in the multipage...)

I don't see a good way to fix this without rewriting our splitting logic :(.
